independent-variation-principle.label: Independent Variation Principle (IVP)
independent-variation-principle.definition:
For a software system S = (F, κ_F, E, Coupling, C, Γ), IVP prescribes the partition induced by the equivalence e₁ ~_Γ e₂ ⇔ Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂): the modules of an IVP-compliant system are the Γ-equivalence classes of the element set. Four conditions make up the structural formulation.
(1) Element Admissibility: every element has at least one change driver, |Γ(e)| ≥ 1.
(2) Element Form: every element is pure (|Γ(e)| = 1) or irreducibly composite.
(3) Separation: elements with different driver assignments reside in different modules, Γ(e₁) ≠ Γ(e₂) ⇒ M(e₁) ≠ M(e₂).
(4) Unification: elements with the same driver assignment reside in the same module, Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂) ⇒ M(e₁) = M(e₂).
independent-variation-principle.also: A driver assignment Γ(e) is the set of change drivers whose variation affects an element, not a single driver. Separation and Unification are the partition content; Admissibility and Element Form constrain the elements themselves.

change-driver.label: Change driver
change-driver.definition: A change driver γ is an equivalence class of domain conditions in the operating domain under the co-variation relation: two conditions belong to the same change driver if they are governed by the same artifact as a single amendment unit, so that revising one obligates revising the other as one change. Co-change in the artifact's revision history is only evidence that the grouping is correct; it is not what makes two conditions one driver. When the change driver's state changes, it creates a requirement for one or more elements of an engineered system to be modified. A change driver must satisfy two constitutive criteria: (1) artifact anchoring — the condition is anchored in a documentable domain artifact; (2) causal pathway — the pathway from the artifact's change to the element's required modification is step-by-step reconstructable. The finite nonempty set of change drivers is C.
change-driver.also: Denoted γ. A change driver's existence is a fact about the domain's causal structure, not a product of having been identified; no design move adds, removes, or transmutes a driver.

change-driver-assignment.label: Change-driver assignment
change-driver-assignment.definition: The assignment function Γ : E → 𝒫(C) maps each element e to its assigned change-driver set Γ(e) ⊆ C — the set of change drivers whose activation requires e to be modified. Each γ ∈ Γ(e) is established by a counterfactual test: if the artifact anchoring γ were rewritten to remove the relevant condition, would the requirement to change e disappear? Equivalently, γ ∈ Γ(e) iff e embodies at least one knowledge piece governed by γ.
change-driver-assignment.also: The causal arrow runs from domain conditions to knowledge to elements: domain conditions govern knowledge, knowledge is embodied by elements, and elements are governed by the change drivers of the knowledge they embody.

element.label: Element
element.definition: An element e ∈ E is any artifact within the system boundary — not only source code (functions, methods, classes, services) but any artifact the system comprises: configuration entries, deployment descriptors and clustering manifests, database schemas, build scripts, infrastructure definitions. The finite set of all elements is E.
element.also: Denoted e ∈ E. An element is pure when it is assigned exactly one driver, composite when more than one.

software-system.label: Software system (tuple)
software-system.definition: A software system S is a 6-tuple S = (F, κ_F, E, Coupling, C, Γ) where F is the functional purpose (the overall goal the system is designed to realize); κ_F ⊆ 𝒦_all is the relevant causal domain knowledge; E is a finite set of elements (artifacts within the system boundary that can change in response to change drivers); Coupling is the coupling relation over element pairs with a coupling dimension and strength; C is a finite set of change drivers, each associated with a knowledge slice κ_γ ⊆ κ_F partitioning κ_F; and Γ : E → 𝒫(C) is the change-driver assignment function.
software-system.also: The first components are inputs read off the domain; Γ is the pivot the principle operates on.

relevant-causal-domain-knowledge.label: Relevant causal domain knowledge
relevant-causal-domain-knowledge.definition: For a system with functional purpose F, the relevant causal domain knowledge is κ_F = {k ∈ K : k is required to realize F} — the finite set of knowledge pieces the system must embody to function correctly. It spans all concern domains required by F. Each knowledge piece k ∈ κ_F has a governing driver set Δ(k) ⊆ C: the change drivers whose activation can force k to change.
relevant-causal-domain-knowledge.also: Denoted κ_F. It is partitioned into knowledge slices, one per leaf-level change driver.

driver-independence.label: Change-driver independence
driver-independence.definition: Two change drivers γ_i and γ_j in C are independent iff γ_i ⊥ γ_j: (1) knowledge disjointness — κ_γᵢ ∩ κ_γⱼ = ∅, the knowledge slices do not overlap; and (2) activation independence — the event that γ_i activates does not logically entail that γ_j activates, and vice versa.
driver-independence.also: Driver independence is a well-formedness condition on the driver set, not a hypothesis IVP requires. Mutually coupled drivers are correctly merged into one.

driver-omission.label: Driver omission
driver-omission.definition: Failing to record a genuine change driver in C. It coarsens the optimal partition and leaves the changes that driver produces uncontained.
driver-omission.also: Omitting a driver is distinct from refinement (splitting or merging drivers), which preserves the structural results.

module.label: Module
module.definition: A module M ⊆ E is a nonempty subset of elements grouped together. The module change-driver set Γ(M) = ⋃_{e∈M} Γ(e) ⊆ C is the union of all change drivers governing the knowledge embodied by M's elements — the set of external conditions that, when they activate, force at least one element of M to change.
module.also: A modularization is a partition of the element set into modules.

modularization.label: Modularization
modularization.definition: A modularization of S is a partition 𝒫 of E into modules: every element belongs to exactly one module, and modules are disjoint. The normative decomposition is the partition P_Γ = E/⧁_Γ — the quotient set of E by the change-driver equivalence relation — the set of all change-driver-equivalence classes [e] = {e' ∈ E : Γ(e') = Γ(e)}.
modularization.also: IVP constrains the modularization through unit purity (IVP-3) and unit completeness (IVP-4).

pure-element.label: Pure element
pure-element.definition: An element e ∈ E* is pure when it is assigned exactly one change driver: |Γ(e)| = 1.
pure-element.also: Denoted e ∈ E* where |Γ(e)| = 1. A pure element is always irreducible.

irreducible-composite.label: Irreducible composite
irreducible-composite.definition: An element e* is irreducibly composite if |Γ(e*)| = n ≥ 2 and both hold: (1) purpose elimination — for every proper subset A ⊊ Γ(e*), restricting e*'s driver assignment to A eliminates the element's purpose entirely; (2) no decomposition exists — there is no partition of e* into sub-elements whose driver sets each have size < n and that jointly preserve the element's purpose.
irreducible-composite.also: Adapters and translators are typically irreducibly composite. An irreducible composite pays an intrinsic multi-driver cost forced by the domain.

coupling.label: Coupling
coupling.definition: An entity e is coupled to every other entity that accesses a resource r that e also accesses — a resource whose definition, state, or capacity e's correct behaviour depends on, and to which at least one other entity's correct behaviour also depends. A coupling is the triple (e₁, r, e₂): two entities together with the resource that links them; the resource r is the medium of the coupling.
coupling.also: Coupling is a standing constraint relation, not an event: it holds whether or not any change ever occurs.

cohesion.label: Cohesion
cohesion.definition: Cohesion is the degree to which a module complies with the partitioning rules that define its decomposition. For a system assessed under k partitioning rules 𝒫 = {R₁, …, Rₖ}, cohesion is measured by a 2k-tuple — one (purity, completeness) pair per rule. A module is fully cohesive iff it scores maximally on every component.
cohesion.also: Causal cohesion arises under the partitioning rule of change-driver-assignment identity (Γ-equivalence).

causal-cohesion.label: Causal cohesion
causal-cohesion.definition: Causal cohesion is the (purity, completeness) pair contributed by the R_Γ slot in the 2k-tuple — the component measuring fidelity to the principle of change-driver-assignment identity (k = 1). Purity (internal uniformity): every element in M shares the same change-driver-assignment set, ∀e₁,e₂∈M: Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂). Completeness (external coverage): no element sharing M's change-driver-assignment set resides outside M, ∀e∈E: Γ(e) ∈ 𝒜(M) ⇒ e ∈ M. A module is causally cohesive iff it is both pure and complete.
causal-cohesion.also: The failure mode of impurity is accidental coupling; the failure mode of incompleteness is shotgun surgery.

cohesion-profile.label: Cohesion profile
cohesion-profile.definition: The cohesion profile of a system assessed under k partitioning rules 𝒫 = {R₁, …, Rₖ} is the 2k-tuple cohesion(M, 𝒫) = (purity₁(M,R₁), completeness₁(M,R₁), …, purityₖ(M,Rₖ), completenessₖ(M,Rₖ)) — one (purity, completeness) pair per rule, each diagnosing fidelity to that rule's partition.
cohesion-profile.also: A module is fully cohesive when it scores maximally on every component of the profile.

partitioning-rule.label: Partitioning rule
partitioning-rule.definition: A partitioning rule R is a rule that assigns every element e ∈ E to exactly one equivalence class Cᵢ ⊆ E, inducing a partition 𝒫_R = {C₁, …, Cₙ} on the element set. The assignment must satisfy four conditions — determinacy, partitionality, externality, and declarativity. A partitioning rule anchors a cohesion metric: purity and completeness are defined relative to the partition it induces.
partitioning-rule.also: The Γ-equivalence rule — group elements by identical change-driver set — is the coarsest partitioning rule that still contains every change to one module.

structural-proxy.label: Structural proxy
structural-proxy.definition: A structural measurement is any function f(e, M, 𝒫, E, R) → V whose input is restricted to structural data — the elements, the dependency relation, and the modularization — and that has no access to the principle P. Observable structural patterns of code (method-call overlap, shared-field density, connected components) correlate with cohesion but cannot define it: a structural measurement is constant on fibers of the structural projection, so it cannot distinguish correct from incorrect placement.
structural-proxy.also: Cohesion proper is correctness relative to a partitioning rule; a structural proxy cannot detect the actual failure mode.

accidental-coupling.label: Accidental coupling
accidental-coupling.definition: An accidental dependency is a dependency that exists in the implementation but is not required by any domain artifact: it lies in R ∖ R_nec. A dependency (e₁, e₂) ∈ R is required when the domain artifact grounding the class assignment of e₁ specifies that e₁ depends on e₂, and no alternative definition of e₁ that omits the reference can satisfy the domain artifact.
accidental-coupling.also: Contrast with necessary coupling, which the domain demands.

necessary-coupling.label: Necessary coupling
necessary-coupling.definition: The necessary dependency graph R_nec ⊆ R is the subset of R consisting of dependencies dictated by the domain under the partitioning principle P — the irreducible coupling floor the system cannot function without.
necessary-coupling.also: Necessary coupling is rule-relative: the same edge one concern demands internal is, under another, demanded external.

resource.label: Resource
resource.definition: A resource is anything whose definition, state, or capacity constrains the elements that share it. A resource has three components: (1) definition — what the resource is (an interface signature, a type, a schema, a pipeline configuration, a team scope, a deployment unit, a CPU allocation); (2) state — the resource's value at a point in time (the implementation behind an interface, the rows in a database, the latency budget consumed by a process); (3) capacity — the limit on concurrent or total access (API rate limits, CPU shares, memory quotas, team headcount). An element accesses a resource when its correct behaviour depends on that resource's definition, state, or capacity.
resource.also: The resource is the medium of a coupling.

visibility-principle.label: Visibility principle
visibility-principle.definition: The principle that coupling should be manifest in the toolchain: every shared resource carries an explicit contract, and violation of the contract is immediately detectable — through a compilation error, a test failure, a build break, a deployment rejection, or a runtime SLO violation.
visibility-principle.also: Reframes the classical 'minimize coupling' imperative: coupling is a standing constraint, so the goal is to make it visible and governed.

variation-dependence.label: Variation dependence
variation-dependence.definition: Two elements e₁, e₂ ∈ E are variation dependent if they share at least one change driver: Γ(e₁) ∩ Γ(e₂) ≠ ∅. The variation class of change driver γ is E_γ = {e ∈ E : γ ∈ Γ(e)} — the elements that must change when γ activates.
variation-dependence.also: Distinct from change-driver equivalence: two elements are change-driver-equivalent exactly when Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂), which is the equivalence relation whose classes form the IVP-compliant partition.

change-driver-equivalence.label: Change-driver equivalence
change-driver-equivalence.definition: Two elements e₁, e₂ ∈ E are change-driver-equivalent, written e₁ ⧁_Γ e₂, iff Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂). The relation ⧁_Γ is an equivalence relation on E (reflexive, symmetric, transitive), so it partitions E into change-driver-equivalence classes [e] = {e' ∈ E : Γ(e') = Γ(e)}. The set of all classes is E/⧁_Γ, the quotient set that forms the IVP-compliant partition.
change-driver-equivalence.also: Distinct from variation dependence: two elements are variation dependent when they share at least one driver (Γ(e₁) ∩ Γ(e₂) ≠ ∅); they are change-driver-equivalent exactly when their driver sets are identical.

domain.label: Domain
domain.definition: A coherent region of causal knowledge. A domain may contain multiple change drivers and decompose into subdomains; at the leaf level it contains exactly one driver.

knowledge-slice.label: Knowledge slice
knowledge-slice.definition: For a set of change drivers D ⊆ C, the knowledge slice governed by D is κ_D = {k ∈ κ_F : Δ(k) ⊆ D} — the set of all knowledge pieces whose governing change drivers are contained in D. For a single change driver γ ∈ C, κ_γ = {k ∈ κ_F : γ ∈ Δ(k)} is the knowledge slice directly governed by γ.
knowledge-slice.also: Denoted κ_γ. There is a bijection between knowledge slices and leaf-level change drivers.

unit-purity.label: Unit Purity
unit-purity.definition: IVP-3 (Separation): elements with different driver assignments belong in different modules — Γ(e₁) ≠ Γ(e₂) ⇒ M(e₁) ≠ M(e₂). Equivalently: no module contains elements with different Γ-assignments.
unit-purity.also: Also called separation of concerns formalized. The failure mode of impurity is accidental coupling.

unit-completeness.label: Unit Completeness
unit-completeness.definition: IVP-4 (Unification): elements with the same driver assignment belong in the same module — Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂) ⇒ M(e₁) = M(e₂). Equivalently: every Γ-equivalence class is contained within a single module.
unit-completeness.also: Also called unification. The failure mode of incompleteness is shotgun surgery.

element-admissibility.label: Element Admissibility
element-admissibility.definition: IVP-1 (Admissibility): every element has at least one change driver — |Γ(e)| ≥ 1 for all e ∈ E. An element with Γ(e) = ∅ is inadmissible: it embodies no part of κ_F and falls outside the system model by definition.

change-driver-assignment-axiom.label: Change-Driver Assignment
change-driver-assignment-axiom.definition: IVP-2 (Element Form): every element is either pure (|Γ(e)| = 1) or irreducibly composite (|Γ(e)| ≥ 2 and irreducible). Reducible composites are excluded: over-broad Γ assignments are corrected upstream, and decomposable elements are split into sub-elements with strictly smaller driver assignments.

partition-theorem.label: Partition Theorem
partition-theorem.definition: The theorem that, under the objective of minimising module-touch count per change-driver activation (with non-zero contamination overhead), the partition P_Γ = E/⧁_Γ — elements grouped by identical Γ-sets — is the unique cost-minimising modularisation of a well-formed element set: no other partition achieves the same minimum. When distinct classes share a change-driver (an irreducible composite), Separation remains optimal among Separation-respecting partitions, but separating the sharing classes is globally strict only when the weighted contamination it removes exceeds the weighted shared-driver span it adds.

software-clustering.label: Software clustering
software-clustering.definition: The problem of recovering or prescribing the modular structure of a software system. Classically an NP-complete optimization over a dependency graph; given the change-driver assignment Γ, the IVP partition is computed in polynomial time.
software-clustering.also: The complexity class tracks the availability of the semantic criterion (Γ), not an intrinsic difficulty of modularisation. When Γ resists identification, structural clustering returns as a hypothesis generator, not a design criterion.

knowledge-theorem.label: Knowledge Theorem
knowledge-theorem.definition: The theorem that cohesion(M, P) = (1, 1) — a module is both pure and complete under a partitioning principle P — holds exactly when M embodies exactly the knowledge of its P-class: cohesion(M,P) = (1,1) ⟺ Knowledge(M) = K_P(Cᵢ), where K_P(Cᵢ) = ⋃_{e∈Cᵢ} Emb(e) is the knowledge embodied collectively by the elements of the P-class Cᵢ that M intersects. Maximal cohesion is maximal knowledge embodiment relative to the principle-determined knowledge grouping.
knowledge-theorem.also: Also called the knowledge-embodiment theorem. It is a result of the cohesion theory, not of IVP itself; IVP supplies one partitioning rule (change-driver identity), while the theorem concerns cohesion in general.

change-management-hypothesis.label: Change Management Hypothesis (CMH)
change-management-hypothesis.definition: The Change Management Hypothesis holds that the primary purpose of modularization is to minimize the economic cost of implementing, verifying, and maintaining the changes a system is required to undergo over its lifetime — and that architectural quality is measured by how well it achieves this. It is a normative postulate stipulating the optimisation objective that any principled modularization theory must adopt.
change-management-hypothesis.also: IVP is derived from CMH. Whether CMH is also an empirically falsifiable prediction about real maintenance costs is a separate question.

shared-resource.label: Shared resource
shared-resource.definition: The coupling medium in the shared-resource account of coupling: two entities are coupled when they both access the same resource — a resource whose definition, state, or capacity both entities' correct behaviour depends on. A coupling is the triple (e₁, r, e₂).
shared-resource.also: Formalizes coupling as a ternary (element, resource, element); Γ is derived from the resource-access and resource-governance mappings.

language-imposed-coupling.label: Language-imposed coupling
language-imposed-coupling.definition: The irreducible residuum of accidental coupling a programming language inflicts on all programs — unavoidable given the language's constructs, even under optimal design.

separation-of-concerns.label: Separation of Concerns (SoC)
separation-of-concerns.definition: The design principle that different concerns should be separated; formalized as an IVP special case when concerns correspond to change drivers.

single-responsibility-principle.label: Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
single-responsibility-principle.definition: The heuristic, attributed to Robert Martin, that a module should have a single reason to change. Martin stated it in three formulations: SRP-1 (one reason, |Γ(M)| = 1), SRP-2 (one actor), and SRP-3 (one business function). Under IVP analysis all three mandate a singular module cardinality, and this claim is false: it makes an unsupported claim about module cardinality. An adapter between two independently governed drivers has |Γ(M)| = 2 and is irreducibly composite — no decomposition into sub-elements with |Γ(eᵢ)| < 2 preserves its purpose — so it violates all three formulations yet cannot be split.

open-closed-principle.label: Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
open-closed-principle.definition: The heuristic that software should be open for extension but closed for modification. Analyzed by IVP as a change-driver consequence under driver hierarchy.

dependency-inversion-principle.label: Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
dependency-inversion-principle.definition: The heuristic that high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Under IVP analysis, DIP changes the placement of a dependency: it relocates the change-propagation boundary onto the abstraction's contract. DIP does not add, remove, or transmute a change driver, and it does not reduce the change-propagation blast radius of any engaged driver — it repositions the boundary the driver propagates across.

liskov-substitution-principle.label: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
liskov-substitution-principle.definition: The behavioral contract principle that subtypes must be substitutable for their base types. Analyzed by IVP through behavioral contracts and variation independence.

interface-segregation-principle.label: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
interface-segregation-principle.definition: The heuristic that clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. Under IVP, ISP is a conditional corollary of DIP applied per client.

grasp.label: GRASP
grasp.definition: Larman's set of nine responsibility-assignment patterns (Information Expert, Creator, Low Coupling, High Cohesion, and others). Under IVP analysis they reduce to one unresolved coupling–cohesion tension.

paradigm.label: Programming paradigm
paradigm.definition: A style or family of languages (object-oriented, functional, procedural, dynamic) that realizes principles through specific constructs; paradigms implement principles rather than define them.

change-driver-partition.label: Change-driver partition
change-driver-partition.definition: The change-driver partition of the element set E groups elements by their change-driver assignment: e₁ and e₂ fall in the same class exactly when Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂). The modules of an IVP-compliant system are these classes. The partition theorem fixes the classes uniquely up to the freedom to subdivide one class, which does not change change containment.
change-driver-partition.also: The partition is read off the domain's causal structure; it is not a selection among equally admissible decompositions.

module-purity.label: Module purity
module-purity.definition: A module M is pure when every element in it carries the same change-driver assignment: ∀e₁, e₂ ∈ M, Γ(e₁) = Γ(e₂). Purity is a property of the module, not of its individual elements. Its failure mode is impurity, which appears as accidental coupling: elements answerable to different drivers share one module.
module-purity.also: A pure module can still be incomplete; purity and completeness are independent components of cohesion.

module-completeness.label: Module completeness
module-completeness.definition: A module M is complete when no element outside it carries an assignment present inside it: ∀e ∈ E, Γ(e) ∈ 𝒜(M) ⇒ e ∈ M, where 𝒜(M) is the set of driver assignments realized in M. Its failure mode is incompleteness, which scatters one class across modules and appears as shotgun surgery: one change forces edits in several places.
module-completeness.also: Completeness is external coverage; purity is internal uniformity. A module can be pure and incomplete at the same time.

faithful-embodiment.label: Faithful embodiment
faithful-embodiment.definition: An element correctly embodies a knowledge piece k when its representation, manipulation, or implementation of k conforms to k. A module correctly embodies k when one of its elements does and none of its elements embodying k deviates. A system satisfies an obligation exactly when every knowledge piece the obligation constrains is correctly embodied by some element; placement does not enter that condition.
faithful-embodiment.also: Presence of knowledge in an element (embodiment) is necessary for correct embodiment but does not entail it.

knowledge-embodiment.label: Knowledge embodiment
knowledge-embodiment.definition: An element embodies a knowledge piece when it represents, manipulates, or implements that piece: a computeTax() method embodies the tax-rate knowledge, a sanitizeInput() method the sanitisation policy. Embodiment records presence only; correct embodiment adds conformance. Which element embodies which piece is a modelling choice at a stated granularity, not an empirical discovery.
knowledge-embodiment.also: Embodiment is the relation between the system's knowledge κ_F and its elements; cohesion measures how well a module's embodiment follows a partitioning rule.

change-propagation.label: Change propagation
change-propagation.definition: Change propagation is what activating one change driver costs a modularization, measured as a pair: the number of modules the change touches (access propagation) and the total count of irrelevant co-residents in those modules (interference propagation).
change-propagation.also: The pair is the objective the partition theorem minimizes; collapsing it to one number requires a weighting convention.

decisional-autonomy.label: Decisional autonomy
decisional-autonomy.definition: Decisional autonomy is the precondition that the organisational unit owning a module can modify, test, and deploy within its scope without cross-unit coordination. It is an organisational property, not a property of the code or of the causal structure.
decisional-autonomy.also: When decisional autonomy fails, the cost model does not capture the coordination overhead, and the derived boundaries need not match decision-making authority.

governing-artifact.label: Governing artifact
governing-artifact.definition: A governing artifact is a regulation, contract, specification, or service-level commitment that imposes obligations on the system. The obligations it states are facts about the domain: the architect has no authority over them, and the architect's derivation of them is a fallible estimate.
governing-artifact.also: Machine and cost knowledge enter the derivation only through obligations that depend on them — a latency SLA in a platform contract, not a preference for speed.

interface-ownership.label: Interface ownership
interface-ownership.definition: An interface is owned by the party that unilaterally controls changes to its specification: only that party's requirements or strategy can add, remove, or modify its methods and contracts. The ownership clause of the Dependency Inversion Principle assigns ownership to the client.
interface-ownership.also: Applied once per client of a shared provider, the ownership clause produces the structure the Interface Segregation Principle prescribes.

design-heuristic.label: Design heuristic
design-heuristic.definition: A design heuristic is an informal rule of design practice: it names a practice or a symptom and recommends a response, without being derived from a model and without supplying a test that decides a case. A principle, in the formal sense, is a theorem derived from an axiomatic system; a heuristic is not.
design-heuristic.also: Robert C. Martin's SOLID rules and packaging rules are heuristics in this sense, which is why the site calls them heuristics rather than principles.

garbage-collection.label: Garbage collection (GC)
garbage-collection.definition: Garbage collection is automatic reclamation of heap storage that the program can no longer reach. The runtime decides when to collect, so the program does not free memory and cannot state exactly when memory returns.

tracing-collector.label: Tracing collector
tracing-collector.definition: A tracing collector finds the objects that are still reachable by following references from the program's roots, and reclaims everything else. It can recover cycles, which reference counting cannot, but it runs on the collector's schedule.

reference-counting.label: Reference counting
reference-counting.definition: Reference counting keeps a count of the handles to each object and frees the object when the count reaches zero. Reclamation is deterministic, but a cycle of references keeps its own count above zero and leaks unless something breaks it.

generational-gc.label: Generational collector
generational-gc.definition: A generational collector separates short-lived objects from long-lived ones and collects the young generation often and cheaply. It assumes that most objects die young, so the common collection is fast and the full one is rare.

ownership-model.label: Ownership model
ownership-model.definition: An ownership model is a static rule that decides which handle owns a value, when the value moves, and when it is released. Rust's borrow checker enforces one; most languages state ownership in comments and leave aliasing unrestricted.

borrow-checker.label: Borrow checker
borrow-checker.definition: The borrow checker is the compiler pass that enforces Rust's ownership rules: a value has one owner, a borrow may be shared or mutable but not both, and a reference may not outlive its referent.

lifetime-parameter.label: Lifetime (Rust)
lifetime-parameter.definition: In Rust a lifetime is the region of code for which a reference is valid. The compiler checks that a reference never outlives the value it points to, and a signature states the relation when it is not obvious.

weak-reference.label: Weak reference
weak-reference.definition: A weak reference points at an object without keeping it alive. It is how a reference cycle is broken so that reference counting can reclaim the objects in it.

autorelease-pool.label: Autorelease pool
autorelease-pool.definition: An autorelease pool defers the release of an Objective-C object until the pool drains. The release therefore happens later than the last reference, which is why Objective-C is charged M2.

buffer-overflow.label: Buffer overflow
buffer-overflow.definition: A buffer overflow writes past the end of an allocation. Without bounds checking it can overwrite adjacent data or control flow, which is why it is charged under Q1.

persistent-data-structure.label: Persistent data structure
persistent-data-structure.definition: A persistent data structure keeps its old version valid after an update, usually by sharing structure with the new one. The immutable collections in Clojure, Scala, and Haskell are persistent.

type-erasure.label: Type erasure
type-erasure.definition: Type erasure removes a type parameter from the artifact, so a list of strings and a list of integers are the same run-time type. A consumer then recovers the type by a cast or a convention, which is what T7 records.

structural-typing.label: Structural typing
structural-typing.definition: Structural typing decides compatibility by the members a type has, not by its name. TypeScript and Go accept a value when it has the required shape, so a type need not declare which interfaces it implements.

duck-typing.label: Duck typing
duck-typing.definition: Duck typing accepts a value because it answers the operations used on it at run time. No declaration holds the set of operations, so a rename fails only when the call runs.

sum-type.label: Sum type
sum-type.definition: A sum type is a value that is exactly one of several alternatives, with the compiler tracking which. Rust's enum, Haskell's data types, and TypeScript's discriminated unions are sum types; their absence is charged under T4.

discriminated-union.label: Discriminated union
discriminated-union.definition: A discriminated union is a sum type whose alternatives share a tag field, so a match on the tag narrows the payload. TypeScript and F# use them to make the handled cases visible to the compiler.

sealed-class.label: Sealed class
sealed-class.definition: A sealed class restricts which types may extend it to the same file or module. Kotlin, Scala, and Java use it with a pattern match to get an exhaustive, checked case distinction.

type-class.label: Type class
type-class.definition: A type class declares an operation that several types may implement, and a generic function may require it. Haskell and Rust, where the construct is a trait, use it to get ad-hoc polymorphism without inheritance.

extension-method.label: Extension method
extension-method.definition: An extension method adds a callable method to a type without changing the type. C#, Kotlin, and Swift use it to attach behaviour to a type the author does not own.

higher-kinded-type.label: Higher-kinded type
higher-kinded-type.definition: A higher-kinded type abstracts over a type constructor rather than a type, so it can be instantiated with a list as well as with an integer. Haskell and Scala support them; most languages do not.

dependent-type.label: Dependent type
dependent-type.definition: A dependent type may mention a value, so the type of a result can depend on an argument. Rocq, Lean, and Idris use them to state a theorem as a type and a proof as its value.

linear-type.label: Linear type
linear-type.definition: A linear type must be used exactly once, and an affine type at most once. Rust's ownership is affine: a value moves rather than being copied, and the compiler rejects a use after the move.

parametric-polymorphism.label: Parametric polymorphism
parametric-polymorphism.definition: Parametric polymorphism is a function or type written once over a type parameter, so it behaves the same for every instantiation. Generics and Haskell's type variables are parametric.

ad-hoc-polymorphism.label: Ad-hoc polymorphism
ad-hoc-polymorphism.definition: Ad-hoc polymorphism selects a different implementation for each type: overloading, a type class, or a trait. It differs from parametric polymorphism, where one implementation serves every type.

pattern-matching.label: Pattern matching
pattern-matching.definition: Pattern matching tests a value's shape and binds its parts in one expression. With a sum type and an exhaustive check it replaces a chain of tests with one checked case distinction.

lazy-evaluation.label: Lazy evaluation
lazy-evaluation.definition: Lazy evaluation defers a computation until its result is needed. It allows infinite structures and avoids work, at the cost of unpredictable space use and a failing expression that is not the one that produced the value.

tail-call.label: Tail call
tail-call.definition: A tail call is a call in the last position of a function. A language with tail-call optimisation reuses the frame, so a loop written as recursion does not grow the stack.

structured-concurrency-term.label: Structured concurrency
structured-concurrency-term.definition: Structured concurrency ties the lifetime of a concurrent task to a lexical scope: the scope does not exit until its tasks finish or are cancelled. It makes a leaked task an error rather than an omission.

virtual-thread.label: Virtual thread
virtual-thread.definition: A virtual thread is a thread the language runtime schedules onto a smaller pool of operating-system threads. Java 21 and Go's goroutines use the idea so a blocking style does not cost one OS thread per task.

green-thread.label: Green thread
green-thread.definition: A green thread is a thread scheduled by the language runtime instead of the operating system. The name is older than virtual thread and describes the same M:N scheduling.

cooperative-scheduling.label: Cooperative scheduling
cooperative-scheduling.definition: Cooperative scheduling switches tasks only where a task yields; preemptive scheduling switches them on a timer. With cooperative scheduling one task that does not yield blocks every other task on the same scheduler, so a blocking call is a coupling to the scheduler.

atomic-operation.label: Atomic operation
atomic-operation.definition: An atomic operation is indivisible with respect to other threads: no observer sees it half-done. Compare-and-swap and atomic add are atomic primitives the language or its runtime exposes.

monitor-lock.label: Monitor
monitor-lock.definition: A monitor pairs one lock with the data it protects and lets a thread wait on a condition inside it. Java's synchronized block and C#'s lock are monitors.

race-condition.label: Race condition
race-condition.definition: A race condition is a result that depends on the order in which threads interleave. A data race is the specific case of two threads reaching one cell without synchronisation.

software-transactional-memory.label: Software transactional memory (STM)
software-transactional-memory.definition: STM groups memory operations into a transaction that commits or retries as a unit. Haskell's STM and Clojure's refs use it so a programmer states what must be consistent rather than which lock to take.

algebraic-effect.label: Algebraic effect
algebraic-effect.definition: An effect is an interaction a computation has with its environment: reading state, performing I/O, raising a failure, or suspending. An algebraic effect is such an operation written without saying who handles it; the caller supplies a handler that interprets it, so the implementation is a parameter rather than a dependency. Unison and OCaml 5 provide them.

codebase-manager.label: Unison Codebase Manager (UCM)
codebase-manager.definition: The UCM is the tool that stores and runs a Unison codebase by content hash. It replaces the file-and-build-step model with a database of definitions.

image-based-persistence.label: Image-based persistence
image-based-persistence.definition: Image-based persistence saves the running object graph as an image and restarts from it. Smalltalk systems work this way, so the program and its state are one artifact.

undefined-behaviour.label: Undefined behaviour (UB)
undefined-behaviour.definition: Undefined behaviour is an operation the language standard leaves with no meaning, so the compiler may assume it never happens. A buffer overrun or a signed overflow in C or C++ is undefined behaviour, and the optimiser may remove the check that would have caught it.

zero-cost-abstraction.label: Zero-cost abstraction
zero-cost-abstraction.definition: A zero-cost abstraction compiles to code as efficient as the hand-written form, so an abstraction need not be paid for at run time. Rust, C++, and Zig aim for it.

hygienic-macro.label: Hygienic macro
hygienic-macro.definition: A hygienic macro expands without capturing or colliding with names at the use site. Scheme's syntax-rules and Rust's macro_rules! are hygienic; a textual macro is not.

three-valued-logic.label: Three-valued logic
three-valued-logic.definition: Three-valued logic adds an unknown value to true and false, so a comparison with NULL is neither true nor false. SQL uses it, which is why x = NULL is not true for any x.

set-based-processing.label: Set-based processing
set-based-processing.definition: Set-based processing states an operation over a whole table and lets the engine choose the loop. A row-by-row cursor states the loop, which couples the result's cost to the plan the programmer wrote.

prototype-chain.label: Prototype chain
prototype-chain.definition: A prototype chain resolves a property by walking from the object to its prototype and onward until the name is found. JavaScript uses it instead of classes, so a change to a prototype reaches every object that inherits from it.

pure-function.label: Pure function
pure-function.definition: A pure function returns the same result for the same arguments and has no observable effect. A language that cannot enforce purity leaves the property to convention, so a caller cannot rely on it.

functional-programming.label: Functional programming
functional-programming.definition: Functional programming builds a program from functions and treats a function as a value. It favours immutability and composition, so a change is a new value rather than a mutation of an existing one.

placement-concept.label: Placement
placement-concept.definition: Placement is which module an element occupies, judged against a partitioning rule P. The placement verdict is correct for an element e in module M exactly when M is the P-class of e. Placement is relative to P: without a stated rule there is no correct or incorrect placement.
placement-concept.also: Placement is distinct from faithful embodiment. A module can be placed exactly right and still fail to realize the knowledge it carries.

derivability-architecture.label: Derivability
derivability-architecture.definition: A design question is architectural exactly when the domain's causal knowledge bears on the answer by restricting which answers the system may take. Derivability classifies each answer: derivable core when the obligations admit exactly one answer, feasible region when they admit several and judgment selects among them, provisional when the available knowledge does not settle the admissible set, and infeasible when the obligations cannot be jointly satisfied.
derivability-architecture.also: Significance becomes definite under derivability: an architectural decision is one the domain's obligations constrain, not one that experts happen to consider important.

beam-runtime.label: BEAM
beam-runtime.definition: The BEAM is the virtual machine that runs Erlang and Elixir. It schedules a very large number of lightweight processes, gives each process a private heap that it collects on its own, and lets one process fail without taking the node down.

jvm-runtime.label: Java Virtual Machine (JVM)
jvm-runtime.definition: The JVM is the virtual machine that executes Java bytecode. It supplies the garbage collector, the JIT compiler, and the thread scheduler that Java, Kotlin, Scala, Groovy, and Clojure share.

clr-runtime.label: Common Language Runtime (CLR)
clr-runtime.definition: The CLR is the .NET virtual machine. It executes C#, F#, and Visual Basic and supplies their garbage collector, JIT compiler, and type system.

evm-runtime.label: Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)
evm-runtime.definition: The EVM is the virtual machine that executes a Solidity contract. Every node runs the same bytecode, so a contract's behaviour is fixed by the chain rather than by an operating system.

arc-memory.label: Automatic Reference Counting (ARC)
arc-memory.definition: ARC is reference counting inserted by the compiler: Swift and Objective-C retain and release an object at the points the compiler chooses. Reclamation is deterministic in the common case, and a strong reference cycle still leaks.

stop-the-world-memory.label: Stop-the-world pause
stop-the-world-memory.definition: A stop-the-world pause suspends every mutator thread while the collector works. Its length is a latency cost the program cannot schedule, which is why a collector that pauses is charged under R2.

raii-memory.label: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization (RAII)
raii-memory.definition: RAII ties a resource's lifetime to an object's lifetime: the constructor acquires the resource and the destructor releases it at scope exit. C++, Rust, and Ada's controlled types provide it, so cleanup is not a written obligation.

destructor-memory.label: Destructor
destructor-memory.definition: A destructor is the code a language runs when an object is destroyed. When it runs at scope exit it ties release to the scope; when it runs at collection, its timing is the collector's.

finalizer-memory.label: Finalizer
finalizer-memory.definition: A finalizer is cleanup code that a collector runs before it reclaims an object. Its timing is the collector's, so it is not a substitute for a scope-bound release.

copy-on-write-memory.label: Copy-on-write
copy-on-write-memory.definition: Copy-on-write shares one buffer between values until one of them writes, then copies. It makes a value cheap to copy while keeping each value independent.

use-after-free-memory.label: Use after free
use-after-free-memory.definition: A use-after-free reads or writes storage that has already been released. A language with manual deallocation cannot prevent it; a language with a lifetime rule can.

double-free-memory.label: Double free
double-free-memory.definition: A double free releases the same allocation twice. The second release corrupts the allocator's own state, and the language does not diagnose it without ownership tracking.

trait-typing.label: Trait
trait-typing.definition: A trait is a named set of methods a type may implement. Rust and Scala use traits for shared behaviour without a base class, and Rust's coherence rules decide where an implementation may live.

mixin-typing.label: Mixin
mixin-typing.definition: A mixin is a set of members added to a class without becoming its base class. Ruby modules, Scala traits, and Dart mixins compose behaviour this way.

coercion-typing.label: Implicit coercion
coercion-typing.definition: A coercion converts a value to another type without a written conversion. C discards the fraction in int i = 3.7 by coercion; a language that requires an explicit cast is not charged T2 for it.

exhaustiveness-typing.label: Exhaustiveness checking
exhaustiveness-typing.definition: Exhaustiveness checking proves that a match handles every alternative of a sum type. Without it a new alternative compiles everywhere and fails only when it is reached.

monad-typing.label: Monad
monad-typing.definition: A monad is a type constructor with a way to wrap a value and a way to chain a step that returns the same constructor. Haskell uses it to sequence effects; Rust's Option and ? operator chain the same way.

functor-typing.label: Functor
functor-typing.definition: A functor is a type constructor whose values can be mapped over while keeping the structure. In Haskell it is a type class; in OCaml the word means a module parameterised by another module.

thunk-feature.label: Thunk
thunk-feature.definition: A thunk is a deferred computation stored as a value. A lazy language builds thunks instead of results, and collecting them burns memory when the value is never forced.

continuation-feature.label: Continuation
continuation-feature.definition: A continuation is the rest of a computation, captured as a value. A delimited continuation captures only the part up to a named boundary, which is the mechanism behind algebraic effects.

memoization-feature.label: Memoization
memoization-feature.definition: Memoization caches a function's result per argument so a repeated call returns without recomputing. It trades memory for time and assumes the function is pure.

actor-model-concurrency.label: Actor model
actor-model-concurrency.definition: In the actor model each unit of concurrency owns its state and communicates only by messages. Erlang, Elixir, and Akka use it, so two actors share no mutable memory.

csp-concurrency.label: Communicating sequential processes (CSP)
csp-concurrency.definition: CSP builds concurrency from processes that share no memory and exchange values over channels. Go's goroutines and Crystal's fibers follow it.

coroutine-concurrency.label: Coroutine
coroutine-concurrency.definition: A coroutine is a function that can suspend at a stated point and resume later. Suspension is cooperative, so one coroutine runs until it yields rather than being preempted.

fiber-concurrency.label: Fiber
fiber-concurrency.definition: A fiber is a lightweight thread of execution scheduled by the language runtime rather than the operating system. Crystal, Ruby, and PHP call their cooperative unit a fiber.

mutex-concurrency.label: Mutex
mutex-concurrency.definition: A mutex is a lock that lets one thread enter a critical section at a time. The language supplies the primitive; the discipline that pairs each shared cell with the right mutex is the programmer's.

semaphore-concurrency.label: Semaphore
semaphore-concurrency.definition: A semaphore counts the permits available to a resource, so up to N threads may proceed at once. A mutex is a semaphore with one permit.

lock-free-concurrency.label: Lock-free
lock-free-concurrency.definition: A lock-free algorithm guarantees that at least one thread makes progress without taking a lock. It uses atomic primitives such as compare-and-swap instead.

compare-and-swap-concurrency.label: Compare-and-swap (CAS)
compare-and-swap-concurrency.definition: Compare-and-swap writes a new value only if the cell still holds an expected value. It is the primitive a lock-free algorithm is built from.

content-addressed-feature.label: Content-addressed code
content-addressed-feature.definition: Content-addressed code names a definition by the hash of its content rather than by a path. Unison works this way, so a change produces a new name and nothing that depended on the old definition breaks silently.

otp-runtime.label: Open Telecom Platform (OTP)
otp-runtime.definition: OTP is the Erlang library of behaviours — GenServer, supervisor, application — that a fault-tolerant node is built from. Elixir uses the same library.

genserver-runtime.label: GenServer
genserver-runtime.definition: A GenServer is an OTP behaviour that turns a process into a server with synchronous calls, asynchronous casts, and a state loop. It is the ordinary unit of state in Erlang and Elixir.

let-it-crash-concurrency.label: Let it crash
let-it-crash-concurrency.definition: Let it crash is the Erlang and Elixir discipline of letting a process fail and restarting it from a known state under a supervisor, rather than handling every error in place.

ets-runtime.label: ETS (Erlang Term Storage)
ets-runtime.definition: ETS is Erlang's in-memory table store, shared between processes and owned by the process that created it. Its lifetime is the owner's, which puts it outside a process's private heap.

nif-runtime.label: Native Implemented Function (NIF)
nif-runtime.definition: A NIF is a function Erlang or Elixir calls from native code. It runs inside the virtual machine, so a slow or crashing NIF can block or take down the scheduler that called it.

ffi-runtime.label: Foreign function interface (FFI)
ffi-runtime.definition: An FFI is the boundary at which one language calls a function written in another. Values must be converted at the boundary, and the called code's guarantees are outside the caller's type system.

abi-runtime.label: Application binary interface (ABI)
abi-runtime.definition: An ABI fixes how compiled code calls compiled code: register use, argument order, name mangling, and struct layout. Two builds that disagree on the ABI cannot link.

rtti-runtime.label: Run-time type information (RTTI)
rtti-runtime.definition: RTTI is type information kept in the artifact so a program can inspect a value's type at run time. It is what reflection and a checked downcast need, and it is what type erasure removes.

simd-runtime.label: Single instruction, multiple data (SIMD)
simd-runtime.definition: SIMD applies one instruction to several values at once. A language or library exposes vector types so a data-parallel loop can use the wider registers.

aslr-runtime.label: Address space layout randomization (ASLR)
aslr-runtime.definition: ASLR places a program's regions at randomised addresses so an attacker cannot rely on a fixed address. It is an operating-system mitigation, not a language one.

bytecode-runtime.label: Bytecode
bytecode-runtime.definition: Bytecode is an intermediate instruction set a compiler emits and a virtual machine executes. It is portable across machines and needs the virtual machine's interpreter or JIT to run.

interpreter-runtime.label: Interpreter
interpreter-runtime.definition: An interpreter executes a program's instructions one at a time instead of compiling them to native code first. It starts instantly and runs slower than compiled or JIT-compiled code.

jit-runtime.label: Just-in-time compilation (JIT)
jit-runtime.definition: A JIT compiles a hot path to native code while the program runs. It reaches compiled speed after a warm-up, so the first requests are slower than the steady state.

aot-runtime.label: Ahead-of-time compilation (AOT)
aot-runtime.definition: AOT compiles the whole program to native code before it runs, so there is no warm-up and no compiler in the deployed artifact. It cannot specialise on run-time values the way a JIT can.

repl-runtime.label: Read-eval-print loop (REPL)
repl-runtime.definition: A REPL reads one expression, evaluates it, prints the result, and waits. It is the interactive entry point of a dynamic language and of GHCi.

monomorphization-feature.label: Monomorphization
monomorphization-feature.definition: Monomorphization compiles a separate copy of a generic function for each type it is used with. It removes dispatch cost and grows the binary, unlike type erasure.

homoiconicity-feature.label: Homoiconicity
homoiconicity-feature.definition: A language is homoiconic when its programs are written in the same structure the language manipulates as data. A Lisp program is a list, so a macro is an ordinary function over that list.

s-expression-feature.label: S-expression
s-expression-feature.definition: An S-expression is a parenthesised prefix form: an operator followed by its arguments, or a literal. Lisp, Scheme, Racket, and Clojure source is a sequence of S-expressions.

clos-feature.label: Common Lisp Object System (CLOS)
clos-feature.definition: CLOS is Common Lisp's object system. It separates a generic function from its methods, which specialise on several arguments, so dispatch is not tied to a class.

srfi-feature.label: Scheme Request for Implementation (SRFI)
srfi-feature.definition: An SRFI is a numbered Scheme specification for a library or a language extension. It lets the small Scheme standard grow without a new standard.

mvcc-data.label: Multiversion concurrency control (MVCC)
mvcc-data.definition: MVCC keeps several versions of a row so a reader sees a consistent snapshot without blocking a writer. PostgreSQL and Oracle use it to trade storage for concurrency.

ddl-data.label: Data definition language (DDL)
ddl-data.definition: DDL is the part of SQL that defines and alters schema objects: CREATE, ALTER, DROP. It is distinct from the statements that read and write rows.

dml-data.label: Data manipulation language (DML)
dml-data.definition: DML is the part of SQL that reads and writes rows: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. It is distinct from the statements that define the schema.

linq-data.label: Language Integrated Query (LINQ)
linq-data.definition: LINQ is C#'s syntax for querying a sequence, a database, or an XML tree through one set of operators. The provider translates the query, so the same expression reaches different execution engines.

ufcs-feature.label: Uniform function call syntax (UFCS)
ufcs-feature.definition: UFCS lets f(x) be written x.f(), so a free function reads as a method. D and Nim use it to attach behaviour to a type without an extension declaration.

trampoline-feature.label: Trampoline
trampoline-feature.definition: A trampoline turns recursion into a loop by returning the next call to a driver instead of making it. It gives constant stack use without a tail-call guarantee from the runtime.

sigil-feature.label: Sigil
sigil-feature.definition: A sigil is a character prefixed to a name to state its kind: Perl's scalar, array, and hash prefixes, or Ruby's @instance. It makes the variable's category visible at every use.

gil-runtime.label: Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)
gil-runtime.definition: The GIL is a single lock that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. It serialises CPU-bound work, so a Python program must use a process pool or a native extension to use a second core.

gvl-runtime.label: Global VM Lock (GVL)
gvl-runtime.definition: The GVL is Ruby's name for the single lock that lets only one thread run Ruby code at a time. It serialises bytecode execution, so a CPU-bound thread must leave the language to use a second core.

reflection-runtime.label: Reflection
reflection-runtime.definition: Reflection lets a program inspect and change its own structure at run time: a type, a field, a method, an annotation. It turns every private member into a reachable one, and it needs type information that erasure would remove.

metaclass-typing.label: Metaclass
metaclass-typing.definition: A metaclass is the class of a class: it decides how instances of the class are created and how method lookup proceeds. Smalltalk, Python, and Groovy expose it, so the object model itself is open to the program.

boxing-memory.label: Boxing
boxing-memory.definition: Boxing stores a primitive value in a heap object so it can be used where an object is required; unboxing copies it back. The conversion costs an allocation and makes a value's identity, not just its contents, observable.

dsl-feature.label: Domain-specific language (DSL)
dsl-feature.definition: A DSL is a small language built for one problem domain, either as its own syntax or as a constrained use of a host language. A macro or a builder API often supplies the syntax inside a general-purpose language.

oop-paradigm.label: Object-oriented programming (OOP)
oop-paradigm.definition: OOP organises a program as objects that hold state and answer operations. It reaches behaviour through inheritance, interfaces, or message passing, and each of those choices fixes a different coupling.

gradual-typing.label: Gradual typing
gradual-typing.definition: Gradual typing lets one program mix checked and unchecked regions: a declaration may state a type and be checked, or leave it dynamic and defer the check to run time. TypeScript and Python's optional annotations work this way.

value-type.label: Value type
value-type.definition: A value type is copied on assignment and on argument passing, so each variable holds its own copy. A reference type shares one object, so a write through one handle is visible through every other.

move-semantics.label: Move semantics
move-semantics.definition: Move semantics transfers a value's ownership instead of copying it, and leaves the source unusable. C++ and Rust use it to release a resource exactly once without a collector.

type-inference.label: Type inference
type-inference.definition: Type inference lets the compiler derive a type the source does not write. It removes annotation noise without removing the check, unless the inferred type falls back to a universal one.

row-polymorphism.label: Row polymorphism
row-polymorphism.definition: Row polymorphism lets a function accept any record that has at least the named fields, while the caller keeps the extra ones. OCaml, PureScript, and TypeScript's structural types express it.

escape-analysis.label: Escape analysis
escape-analysis.definition: Escape analysis decides whether an allocation can stay on the stack because no reference to it leaves the function. Go and the JVM use it to remove heap allocation and the collection cost that follows.

null-safety-typing.label: Null safety
null-safety-typing.definition: Null safety makes possible absence part of the type, so a reference either excludes the absent value or says it may hold it. Kotlin's String? and Swift's optionals are the construct; a language without it lets any reference be absent.

allocator-memory.label: Allocator
allocator-memory.definition: An allocator is the component that reserves and releases memory. A language that passes an allocator explicitly, as Zig does, lets a caller choose where a value lives instead of coupling it to one global heap.

scheduler-concurrency.label: Scheduler
scheduler-concurrency.definition: A scheduler decides which runnable task runs next and on which thread. When the language runtime owns the scheduler, a blocking call couples the task to the scheduler's policy.

channel-concurrency.label: Channel
channel-concurrency.definition: A channel is a queue that passes values between concurrent tasks without shared memory. CSP languages and Go use it, so communication is a stated operation rather than a shared cell.

thread-local-concurrency.label: Thread-local storage
thread-local-concurrency.definition: Thread-local storage gives each thread its own copy of a value, so two threads do not share the cell. It is the explicit escape from shared mutable state, and it must be requested rather than assumed.
